{{Short description|Topology made of cocountable subsets}}
The '''cocountable topology''', also known as the '''countable complement topology''', is a [[topology]] that can be defined on any [[infinite set]] <math>X</math>. In this topology, a set is [[open set|open]] if its [[set complement|complement]] in <math>X</math> is either countable or equal to the entire set. Equivalently, the open sets consist of the [[empty set]] and all subsets of <math>X</math> whose complements are countable, a property known as [[cocountable|cocountability]]. The only [[closed set]]s in this topology are <math>X</math> itself and the countable subsets of <math>X</math>.

==Definitions==
Let <math> X </math> be an [[infinite set]] and let <math> \mathcal{T} </math> be the set of [[subsets]] of <math> X </math> such that <math display=block> H \in \mathcal{T} \iff X \setminus H \mbox{ is countable, or}\, H = \varnothing </math> then <math> \mathcal{T} </math> is the countable complement topology on <math> X </math>, and the [[topological space]] <math> T = ( X , \mathcal{T} ) </math> is a countable complement space.<ref name="Munkres">{{Cite book |last=Munkres |first=James Raymond |author-link=James Munkres |title=Topology |date=2000 |publisher=Prentice Hall |isbn=0-13-181629-2 |edition=2nd |location=Upper Saddle River (N. J.)}}</ref>

Symbolically, the topology is typically written as
<math display=block>\mathcal{T} = \{H \subseteq X : H = \varnothing \mbox{ or } X \setminus H \mbox{ is countable} \}.</math>

===Double pointed cocountable topology===
Let <math>X</math> be an [[uncountable set]]. We define the topology <math>\mathcal{T}</math> as all open sets whose complements are countable, along with <math>\varnothing</math> and <math>X</math> itself.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Steen |first=Lynn Arthur |title=Counterexamples in Topology |last2=Seebach, Jr. |first2=J. Arthur |date=1978 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=978-1-4612-6290-9 |edition=2nd |location=New York, NY |page=50 |language=en |chapter=2}}</ref>

===Cocountable extension topology===
Let <math>X</math> be the real line. Now let <math>\mathcal{T}_1</math>  be the [[Euclidean topology]] and <math>\mathcal{T}_2</math> be the cocountable topology on <math>X</math>. The ''cocountable extension topology'' is the smallest topology generated by <math>\mathcal{T}_1 \cup \mathcal{T}_2</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Steen |first=Lynn Arthur |title=Counterexamples in Topology |last2=Seebach, Jr. |first2=J. Arthur |date=1978 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=978-1-4612-6290-9 |edition=2nd |location=New York, NY |page=85 |language=en |chapter=2}}</ref>

==Proof that cocountable topology is a topology== 
By definition, the [[empty set]] <math> \varnothing </math> is an element of <math>\mathcal{T}</math>. Similarly, the entire set <math> X \in \mathcal{T} </math>, since the [[Set complement|complement]] of <math> X </math> relative to itself is the empty set, which is [[vacuously]] countable.

Suppose <math>A, B \in \mathcal{T}</math>. Let <math>H = A \cap B</math>. Then

<math>
X \setminus H = X \setminus (A \cap B) = (X \setminus A) \cup (X \setminus B)
</math>

by [[De Morgan's laws#Set theory| De Morgan's laws]]. Since <math>A, B \in \mathcal{T}</math>, it follows that <math>X \setminus A</math> and <math>X \setminus B</math> are both countable. Because the countable union of countable sets is countable, <math>X \setminus H</math> is also countable. Therefore, <math>H = A \cap B \in \mathcal{T}</math>, as its complement is countable.

Now let <math>\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}</math>. Then

<math>
X \setminus \left( \bigcup \mathcal{U} \right) = \bigcap_{U \in \mathcal{U}} (X \setminus U)
</math>

again by De Morgan's laws. For each <math>U \in \mathcal{U}</math>, <math>X \setminus U</math> is countable. The countable intersection of countable sets is also countable (assuming <math>\mathcal{U}</math> is countable), so <math>S \setminus \left( \bigcup \mathcal{U} \right)</math> is countable. Thus, <math>\bigcup \mathcal{U} \in \mathcal{T}</math>.

Since all three [[Topological space#Definition via open sets|open set axioms]] are met, <math>\mathcal{T}</math> is a topology on <math>X</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Steen |first=Lynn Arthur |title=Counterexamples in Topology |last2=Seebach |first2=J. Arthur |date=1978 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=978-0-387-90312-5 |edition=2nd |location=New York, NY |language=en |chapter=20}}</ref>

==Properties==
Every set <math>X</math> with the cocountable topology is [[Lindelöf space|Lindelöf]], since every nonempty [[open set]] omits only countably many points of <math>X</math>. It is also [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub>]], as all singletons are closed. 

If <math>X</math> is an uncountable set, then any two nonempty open sets [[set intersection|intersect]], hence, the space is not [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]]. However, in the cocountable topology all convergent sequences are eventually constant, so limits are unique. Since [[compact space|compact sets]] in <math>X</math> are finite subsets, all compact subsets are closed, another condition usually related to the Hausdorff separation axiom.

The cocountable topology on a countable set is the [[discrete topology]]. The cocountable topology on an uncountable set is [[hyperconnected space|hyperconnected]], thus [[connected space|connected]], [[locally connected space|locally connected]] and [[pseudocompact space|pseudocompact]], but neither [[limit point compact|weakly countably compact]] nor [[metacompact space|countably metacompact]], hence not compact.

==Examples==
*Uncountable set: On any uncountable set, such as the real numbers <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, the cocountable topology is a proper subset of the [[standard topology]]. In this case, the topology is T<sub>1</sub> but not Hausdorff, first-countable, nor [[metrizable]].

*Countable set (possibly finite): If <math>X</math> is countable, then every subset of <math>X</math> has a countable complement. In this case, the cocountable topology is just the [[discrete topology]].

*Subspace topology: If <math>Y \subseteq X</math> and <math>X</math> carries the cocountable topology, then <math>Y</math> inherits the [[subspace topology]]. This topology on <math>Y</math> consists of the empty set,  all of <math>Y</math>, and all subsets <math>U \subseteq Y</math> such that <math>Y \setminus U</math> is countable.
